transcript:
This message comes from Kachava. A little boost goes a long way, especially when it comes to caring for your gut during the holiday season and beyond.
Introducing Kachava's new 3-in-1 digestive boost. Simply mix into your favorite Kachava shake or any cold beverage.
Go to kachava.com and use code NPR for 15% off your first order. That's K-A-C-H-A-V-A.com. Code NPR.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janene Herbst. President Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 of the U.S.'s major trading partners, including China, Japan, and the European Union, saying it's to fight unfair trade practices, and here's Danielle Kurtzleben has more.
These are being implemented under a law known for short as Section 301, which is meant to counter other countries' unfair trade practices.
And so here, the White House is alleging that these other countries have what's called structural excess capacity in various manufactured goods.
And the administration has described this as when another country has policies that cause a good to be overproduced, which then distorts a global market for that good.
And here's Danielle Kurtzleben reporting. The exact rate isn't known, but they could go as high as 40% on Chinese goods, 35% on goods from Vietnam, and 20% or 25% on goods from other countries.
They could go into effect within a couple of months. The Army destroyed nearly five tons of hazardous chemicals at an ammunition plant in Iowa yesterday.
Tom Barton from Iowa Public Radio reports federal crews are checking how far lead dust may have spread.
The Army used sand barriers, walls of water tanks, tarps, screens, and foam to try and contain the blast and toxic dust.
The EPA collected more than 1,000 air, soil, and water samples before the blast and is still testing alongside local health officials and local universities.
NASA is gathering atmospheric data using research planes and a satellite instrument.
Iowa Poison Control says those results can help people who may have been exposed decide with their doctor whether they need a blood test.
The detonation plant set off a wave of anxiety, evacuations, and preparation in surrounding communities.
For NPR News, I'm Tom Barton in Des Moines.
The Macy's Thanksgiving Parade in New York City has been postponed for the first time until Saturday because of a coastal storm moving up the east coast that's bringing heavy rain and high winds.
This is out of an abundance of caution for the marchers, parades, and giant balloon handlers.
And if you're traveling for Thanksgiving this holiday week, odds are you're driving.
And here's Joe Hernandez says travel experts say the U.S. could see near record levels of travel this holiday.
AAA estimates that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home this Thanksgiving.
It's a slight drop from last year, which the group attributes to higher gas prices.
Most people will drive or fly to wherever they're going, but AAA says both of those groups are declining this year.
What's increasing is the number of people who are taking other modes of transportation, like cruises, buses, and trains.
Amtrak says it broke ridership records during the Thanksgiving holiday period last year and expects to do so again this week.
Joe Hernandez, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un called for his country to focus on the development of tactical nuclear weapons for use on the battlefield.
And here's Anthony Kuhn reports from Seoul on Kim's remarks while touring three separate nuclear-related facilities.
North Korean state media showed pictures of Kim inspecting nuclear warheads and centrifuges for making nuclear fuel on Wednesday.
Kim urged his country to focus on using tactical nuclear weapons for different missions and environments.
The North has developed or is developing means to deliver low-yield nuclear warheads from the land, air, and sea.
Kim said that any attempt to deny or negate the North's status as a nuclear power will be seen as an open declaration of war.
He added that he does not seek international approval or recognition for North Korea's nuclear status,
suggesting that he just wants foreign governments to accept it as an established fact.
Anthony Kuhn in PR News, Seoul.
A federal judge has agreed to block the FCC from conducting an early review of ABC's broadcast license.
The network accuses the FCC of violating its free speech rights and retaliation against programming decisions that the Trump administration dislikes.
U.S. District Judge Lauren Ali Khan granted Disney ABC's parent companies request for a temporary restraining order
and a preliminary injunction on First Amendment grounds.
The license review is part of the Trump administration's campaign to punish media companies for what it sees as liberal bias.
The FCC calls the decision wrong on the facts and wrong on the law.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News, in Washington.
dot com code NPR.
